text: Of things some are in our power, and others are not.
context: The opening line of Epictetus' handbook. Everything else in Stoic practice follows from sorting life into what we can govern (our judgments, intentions, actions) and what we cannot (other people, reputation, outcomes).
prompt: What are you carrying today that was never yours to control?

text: The highest excellence is like (that of) water. The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving (to the contrary), the low place which all men dislike.
context: Water is Taoism's favourite teacher: it nourishes everything, never fights, and settles where nobody else wants to be.
prompt: Where could you be more like water today?

text: By doing just actions we come to be just; by doing the actions of self-mastery we come to be perfected in self-mastery; and by doing brave actions brave.
context: The heart of virtue ethics: we are not born good or bad; we become what we practise, the way a harpist becomes a harpist by playing.
prompt: What quality are you practising, whether you mean to or not?

text: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts. If a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage.
context: The first verse of the Dhammapada, a collection of sayings attributed to the Buddha. It places the mind at the root of experience: the way we habitually think shapes who we become.
prompt: Which thought have you repeated so often that it now feels like a fact?

text: Of all the means which are procured by wisdom to ensure happiness throughout the whole of life, by far the most important is the acquisition of friends.
context: Epicurus lived with his friends in a community called the Garden. For him, friendship was not an extra in a good life but its foundation.
prompt: Which friendship deserves more of your attention than it has been getting?

text: Act only on that maxim whereby thou canst at the same time will that it should become a universal law.
context: Kant's 'categorical imperative', the test at the heart of his ethics: could you want everyone to do what you are about to do?
prompt: What would happen if everyone did what you are tempted to do today?

text: The current of a running stream flows on unceasingly, but the water is not the same: the foam floating on the pool where it lingers, now vanishes and now forms again, but is never lasting. Such are mankind and their habitations.
context: The famous opening of Hōjōki ('An Account of My Ten-Foot Hut', 1212), written by a poet who withdrew to a tiny mountain hut after years of fire, famine and earthquake.
prompt: What in your life is the same river, but different water?

text: The unexamined life is not worth living.
context: Socrates says this at his trial in Athens, having been offered the chance to live if he stops questioning people. He chooses the examined life, even at the cost of his own.
prompt: What part of your life have you stopped questioning?

text: It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.
context: Mill's answer to critics who called utilitarianism a 'philosophy for pigs'. Not all pleasures are equal: the pleasures of thought and feeling are worth more.
prompt: Which of your pleasures are 'higher', and which are just easy?

text: Ready must thou be to burn thyself in thine own flame; how couldst thou become new if thou have not first become ashes!
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra I, 'The Way of the Creating One'
context: Zarathustra speaks to someone setting out on their own path. Real renewal asks us to let an old self burn away.
prompt: What old version of yourself might need to become ashes?

text: Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application? Is it not delightful to have friends coming from distant quarters? Is he not a man of complete virtue, who feels no discomposure though men may take no note of him?
context: The opening lines of the Analects, the sayings of Confucius collected by his students. Learning, friendship and not needing recognition: the whole book in three questions.
prompt: Which of the three would make today a good day: learning something, seeing a friend, or not needing to be noticed?

text: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things; for example, death is nothing terrible, for if it were it would have seemed so to Socrates; for the opinion about death that it is terrible, is the terrible thing.
context: Epictetus, born a slave, taught that suffering often lives in our interpretation of events rather than in the events themselves. Change the judgment and the disturbance changes with it.
prompt: What story are you telling yourself about something that upset you recently?

text: You cannot speak of ocean to a well-frog,—the creature of a narrower sphere. You cannot speak of ice to a summer insect,—the creature of a season.
context: The Spirit of the Ocean speaks to a river god who thought himself great. A frog at the bottom of a well takes its circle of sky for the whole sky.
prompt: Which well are you looking up from, and how big is the sky beyond it?

text: For as it is not one swallow or one fine day that makes a spring, so it is not one day or a short time that makes a man blessed and happy.
context: Aristotle's happiness (eudaimonia) is not a mood but a whole life lived well. One good day doesn't make it, and one bad day doesn't break it.
prompt: What would a good life look like if you judged it by years, not days?

text: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule.
context: Presented not as a new commandment but as an 'old rule', a law of how things work. Answering hostility with hostility only feeds the cycle.
prompt: Is there a resentment you are keeping alive by feeding it?

text: Death, therefore, the most awful of evils, is nothing to us, seeing that, when we are, death is not come, and, when death is come, we are not.
context: Epicurus wanted to free people from the fear of death, which he saw as poisoning ordinary life. Where we are, death is not; where death is, we are not.
prompt: If fear of an ending were set aside, how would you spend this day?

text: Two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe, the oftener and the more steadily we reflect on them: the starry heavens above and the moral law within.
source: Kant, Critique of Practical Reason, Conclusion
context: Kant's most famous sentence, later engraved on his tombstone. The vastness outside us and the sense of right within us are equally worthy of wonder.
prompt: When did you last feel awe, at the sky or at someone's goodness?

text: Those who cannot feel the littleness of great things in themselves are apt to overlook the greatness of little things in others.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. I
context: Okakura wrote The Book of Tea in English in 1906 to explain Japanese culture to the West through the humble act of drinking tea.
prompt: What small thing in someone else have you overlooked?

text: He knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know.
context: Socrates explains why the oracle called him the wisest man in Athens: not because he knew more, but because he was honest about the limits of what he knew.
prompt: Where are you most certain — and what would it cost to be less so?

text: Ask yourself whether you are happy, and you cease to be so. The only chance is to treat, not happiness, but some end external to it, as the purpose of life.
context: Mill learned this from his own depression at twenty. Happiness, he concluded, comes most surely when we aim at something else.
prompt: What could you care about today so much that you forget to check if you're happy?

text: One must still have chaos in one, to give birth to a dancing star.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra, Prologue 5
context: Zarathustra warns against a life made so comfortable and orderly that nothing new can arise from it. Inner turmoil can be the raw material of creation.
prompt: What unsettled part of you might be the beginning of something?

text: I daily examine myself on three points:— whether, in transacting business for others, I may have been not faithful;— whether, in intercourse with friends, I may have been not sincere;— whether I may have not mastered and practised the instructions of my teacher.
context: Zengzi, one of Confucius' students, describes his daily review: Was I reliable for others? Was I sincere with friends? Did I practise what I was taught?
prompt: Run through Zengzi's three questions for today. Which one makes you pause?

text: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial.
context: Written by a Roman emperor in a private notebook. Not cynicism but preparation: he goes on to say such people act from ignorance, and that he cannot be harmed by them or angry with his own kin.
prompt: Who might test your patience today, and how do you want to meet them?

text: He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent. He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes himself is mighty. He who is satisfied with his lot is rich; he who goes on acting with energy has a (firm) will.
context: Four short contrasts between outer and inner achievement. Self-knowledge and self-mastery come out ahead every time.
prompt: Which kind of strength are you building: over others, or over yourself?

text: To be angry, to give money, and be expensive, is what any man can do, and easy: but to do these to the right person, in due proportion, at the right time, with a right object, and in the right manner, this is not as before what any man can do, nor is it easy; and for this cause goodness is rare, and praiseworthy, and noble.
context: Anyone can feel anger or give money. Doing it to the right person, in the right measure, at the right time and in the right way is the real skill.
prompt: Where does a feeling of yours need better aim rather than suppression?

text: As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise.
context: Praise and blame are counted among the 'eight worldly winds' in Buddhist teaching, along with gain and loss, fame and disrepute, pleasure and pain. The wise remain steady in all of them.
prompt: How much of your mood today depends on what others think of you?

text: Let no one be slow to seek wisdom when he is young nor weary in the search thereof when he is grown old. For no age is too early or too late for the health of the soul.
context: The opening of Epicurus' letter summarising his ethics. Philosophy, for him, was a lifelong practice of caring for the soul, never too early and never too late.
prompt: What are you still curious to learn about how to live?

text: So act as to treat humanity, whether in thine own person or in that of any other, in every case as an end withal, never as means only.
context: Kant's second formulation of the moral law: never use a person, including yourself, merely as a tool.
prompt: Is there anyone you've been treating more as a means than as a person?

text: The perfect circle of the full moon lasts only for a very short time; soon it begins to wane, though one who pays no attention to it may think that in a single night there is little or no change perceptible.
context: Kenkō was a 14th-century poet and monk whose short essays on beauty and impermanence remain beloved in Japan. Change, he notes, is often too slow to see.
prompt: What is quietly changing in your life, too slowly to notice?

text: The beginning is the most important part of any work, especially in the case of a young and tender thing; for that is the time at which the character is being formed and the desired impression is more readily taken.
context: Said in a discussion of how to educate the young: early impressions shape everything that follows. The point applies just as well to habits, projects and days.
prompt: How do you want to begin what comes next?

text: If all mankind minus one, were of one opinion, and only one person were of the contrary opinion, mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one person, than he, if he had the power, would be justified in silencing mankind.
context: Mill's classic defence of free expression. A lone dissenter may be right, and even if wrong, their challenge keeps the truth alive.
prompt: Whose minority opinion deserves a fairer hearing from you?

text: I need to discover a Truth which is a Truth for me; I need to find the idea for which I can live and die.
context: Written at twenty-two, on a summer stay by the sea. Kierkegaard, often called the first existentialist, wanted not a system to admire but a truth he could live by.
prompt: What idea would you be willing to build your life around?

text: I will not be afflicted at men's not knowing me; I will be afflicted that I do not know men.
context: Confucius turns a common worry around. Instead of fretting that others don't understand us, he asks whether we understand them.
prompt: Who in your life might you not yet really know?

text: The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong-doer.
context: One of the shortest entries in the Meditations. Being wronged offers a choice: to copy the wrong, or to remain who you are.
prompt: Has someone's behaviour been quietly changing yours?

text: The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space (for the axle), that the use of the wheel depends. Clay is fashioned into vessels; but it is on their empty hollowness, that their use depends. The door and windows are cut out (from the walls) to form an apartment; but it is on the empty space (within), that its use depends.
context: Wheels, bowls and rooms are useful because of what is empty in them. Emptiness is not nothing; it is room.
prompt: Where could some emptiness make your life more useful, not less?

text: No one would choose to live without friends though he should have all the other good things in the world.
context: Two of the ten books of the Ethics are about friendship. For Aristotle it is not a luxury of the good life but part of what makes it good.
prompt: Who would make your life poorer if they were gone?

text: If one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors.
context: From the chapter on 'thousands'. Mastery of one's own mind is placed above any outward victory.
prompt: What small inner victory would matter most today?

text: Nature’s wealth at once has its bounds and is easy to procure; but the wealth of vain fancies recedes to an infinite distance.
context: Natural needs are few and easily met. Desires born of imagination keep moving out of reach however much we acquire.
prompt: Which of your wants keeps receding the closer you get?

text: Nothing can possibly be conceived in the world, or even out of it, which can be called good, without qualification, except a good will.
context: The opening of Kant's argument. Talents, courage and even happiness can be misused. Only a good will is good in every circumstance.
prompt: What good quality of yours depends on good will to stay good?

text: Teaism is a cult founded on the adoration of the beautiful among the sordid facts of everyday existence. It inculcates purity and harmony, the mystery of mutual charity, the romanticism of the social order. It is essentially a worship of the Imperfect, as it is a tender attempt to accomplish something possible in this impossible thing we know as life.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. I
context: Okakura's definition of the tea ceremony's spirit: finding beauty in ordinary life, and honouring what is imperfect.
prompt: Where could you find beauty in the ordinary today?

text: Wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder.
context: Socrates says this to the young Theaetetus, who admits he is dizzy with puzzlement. Confusion is not a failure; it is where real thinking starts.
prompt: What has made you wonder recently?

text: The creed which accepts as the foundation of morals, Utility, or the Greatest Happiness Principle, holds that actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, wrong as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness.
context: The founding principle of utilitarianism, developed by Jeremy Bentham and refined by Mill: judge actions by how much happiness and suffering they bring.
prompt: Whose happiness will your choices touch today?

text: Above all, don’t lie to yourself. The man who lies to himself and listens to his own lie comes to such a pass that he cannot distinguish the truth within him, or around him, and so loses all respect for himself and for others.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book II, ch. 2
context: Advice from the elder Zosima. Dostoevsky is often read as a forerunner of existentialism for his focus on freedom, conscience and self-deception. A century later, Sartre called this kind of self-deception 'bad faith': pretending we have no choice.
prompt: What small lie have you been telling yourself?

text: If a man keeps cherishing his old knowledge, so as continually to be acquiring new, he may be a teacher of others.
context: Good teachers keep returning to what they know until it yields something new. Old knowledge is not a shelf but a garden.
prompt: What do you already know that might teach you something new if you went back to it?

text: We do not have a very short time assigned to us, but we lose a great deal of it … we do not receive a short life, but we make it a short one, and we are not poor in days, but wasteful of them.
source: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 1
context: Seneca wrote this essay to his friend Paulinus. Life, he argues, is long enough if we know how to use it; it only feels short because we give so much of it away.
prompt: Where did your time go yesterday, and was it given or taken?

text: Once upon a time, I, Chuang Tzŭ, dreamt I was a butterfly, fluttering hither and thither, to all intents and purposes a butterfly. I was conscious only of following my fancies as a butterfly, and was unconscious of my individuality as a man. Suddenly, I awaked, and there I lay, myself again. Now I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly dreaming I am a man.
context: The most famous passage in Taoist literature. Zhuangzi wonders how firm the line really is between who we think we are and what we experience.
prompt: What are you sure about that might be less solid than it seems?

text: Easy to miss the mark, but hard to hit it: and for these reasons, therefore, both the excess and defect belong to Vice, and the mean state to Virtue; for, as the poet has it, “Men may be bad in many ways, But good in one alone.”
context: Virtue lies in a 'mean' between too much and too little, and there are many ways to miss it, but only one way to hit it.
prompt: Where are you erring on the side of too much, or too little?

text: Let no man think lightly of evil, saying in his heart, It will not come nigh unto me. Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the fool becomes full of evil, even if he gather it little by little.
context: The verse that follows makes the same point about good. Character is built drop by drop, through small acts we hardly notice.
prompt: What small habit is slowly filling your pot?

text:
'Tis sweet, when, down the mighty main, the winds
Roll up its waste of waters, from the land
To watch another's labouring anguish far,
Not that we joyously delight that man
Should thus be smitten, but because 'tis sweet
To mark what evils we ourselves be spared;
'Tis sweet, again, to view the mighty strife
Of armies embattled yonder o'er the plains,
Ourselves no sharers in the peril; but naught
There is more goodly than to hold the high
Serene plateaus, well fortressed by the wise,
Whence thou may'st look below on other men
And see them ev'rywhere wand'ring, all dispersed
In their lone seeking for the road of life.
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things II
context: Lucretius, a Roman poet, set Epicurus' philosophy to verse. Here he describes the calm of a mind that has found its footing, looking out on a restless world.
prompt: Where is your 'serene plateau' when life gets stormy?

text: Like a jewel, it would still shine by its own light, as a thing which has its whole value in itself.
context: Even if a good intention fails completely, says Kant, its worth is untouched. Its value doesn't depend on results.
prompt: Which of your efforts failed, yet still shone by its own light?

text: A certain man who was learning archery faced the target with two arrows in his hand. But his instructor said, ‘A beginner ought never to have a second arrow; for as long as he relies upon the other, he will be careless with his first one. At each shot he ought to think that he is bound to settle it with this particular shaft at any cost.’
context: A teacher tells his student to carry only one arrow, because a second one makes the first careless. Kenkō applies it to every moment of life.
prompt: What 'second arrow' is making you careless with the first?

text: Then would you rather suffer than do injustice? — I should not like either, but if I must choose between them, I would rather suffer than do.
context: Socrates shocks his companions by arguing that doing wrong damages the soul far more than being wronged does.
prompt: Is there a wrong you could avoid doing, even at some cost to yourself?

text: When people who are tolerably fortunate in their outward lot do not find in life sufficient enjoyment to make it valuable to them, the cause generally is, caring for nobody but themselves.
context: Mill's diagnosis of why comfortable lives can feel empty: selfishness narrows life until little in it seems worth having.
prompt: Who, beyond yourself, could you care more about?

text: All the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.
context: Pascal, a 17th-century mathematician and religious thinker, anticipated the existentialists' focus on restlessness and distraction.
prompt: Could you sit quietly, alone, for ten minutes today?

text: Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous.
context: Reading without reflecting changes nothing; reflecting without learning goes round in circles. Confucius wants both, together.
prompt: Are you lately more at risk of learning without thinking, or thinking without learning?

text: Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, sea-shores, and mountains; and thou too art wont to desire such things very much. But this is altogether a mark of the most common sort of men, for it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself.
context: Marcus reminds himself that the quiet he longs for in the countryside is always available within. The retreat is a practice, not a place.
prompt: Where in yourself can you retreat to, right now, for a minute?

text: The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout; the tower of nine storeys rose from a (small) heap of earth; the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
context: The source of the saying 'a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step'. A li is a traditional Chinese measure of distance.
prompt: What is the single step you could take today?

text: The Virtues then come to be in us neither by nature, nor in despite of nature, but we are furnished by nature with a capacity for receiving them and are perfected in them through custom.
context: We have a natural capacity for goodness, but it only becomes real through practice, the way a seed needs tending.
prompt: Which of your good capacities is waiting for practice?

text: He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me,"—in those who harbour such thoughts hatred will never cease. "He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me,"—in those who do not harbour such thoughts hatred will cease."
context: Two nearly identical verses that differ by a single word. Hatred lives on in the stories we rehearse about the wrongs done to us.
prompt: Which old grievance do you still replay, and what would happen if you stopped?

text: Accustom thyself to believe that death is nothing to us, for good and evil imply sentience, and death is the privation of all sentience; therefore a right understanding that death is nothing to us makes the mortality of life enjoyable, not by adding to life an illimitable time, but by taking away the yearning after immortality.
context: The goal is not to make life longer but to make mortal life enjoyable, by letting go of the craving to live forever.
prompt: How would you live if you made peace with being mortal?

text: In the kingdom of ends everything has either value or dignity. Whatever has a value can be replaced by something else which is equivalent; whatever, on the other hand, is above all value, and therefore admits of no equivalent, has a dignity.
context: Things have a price and can be swapped. People have dignity: they cannot be replaced by anything 'equivalent'.
prompt: Where have you been putting a price on something that has dignity?

text: Let us dream of evanescence, and linger in the beautiful foolishness of things.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. I
context: The closing line of Okakura's first chapter: an invitation to slow down and savour what passes.
prompt: What passing thing could you linger over today?

text: Be of good cheer about death, and know of a certainty, that no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death.
context: Socrates' words to the jurors who voted to acquit him. A good person's integrity cannot be taken from them by anything that happens.
prompt: What in you can no misfortune touch?

text: He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.
context: To hold an opinion well, you must understand the best arguments against it.
prompt: Can you state the strongest case against a view you hold?

text: In one’s friend one shall have one’s best enemy. Thou shalt be closest unto him with thy heart when thou withstandest him.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra I, 'The Friend'
context: For Nietzsche, a true friend challenges us rather than flatters us, and we are closest to them when we push back.
prompt: Which friend challenges you, and do you challenge them?

text: When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it;— this is knowledge.
context: Spoken to Zilu, a bold student who was quick to speak. Like Socrates, Confucius places wisdom in being honest about where our knowledge ends.
prompt: Where do you pretend to know more than you do?

text: Take away thy opinion, and then there is taken away the complaint, "I have been harmed." Take away the complaint, "I have been harmed," and the harm is taken away.
context: A compressed version of the Stoic method: the injury we feel is bound up with the judgment that we have been injured.
prompt: Which 'I have been harmed' could you set down today?

text: Sincere words are not fine; fine words are not sincere.
context: The opening line of the last chapter. Polish can be a sign that something is being sold rather than said.
prompt: Whose plain words have you overlooked because they weren't polished?

text: Every art, and every science reduced to a teachable form, and in like manner every action and moral choice, aims, it is thought, at some good: for which reason a common and by no means a bad description of the Chief Good is, “that which all things aim at.”
context: The first sentence of the Ethics. Everything we do aims at some good, so the real question is: what is the highest good, the one we want for its own sake?
prompt: What are your daily actions ultimately aiming at?

text: The world does not know that we must all come to an end here;—but those who know it, their quarrels cease at once.
context: Remembering that every life ends puts most quarrels in proportion.
prompt: Which disagreement would fade if you remembered how short life is?

text: And even as men choose of food not merely and simply the larger portion, but the more pleasant, so the wise seek to enjoy the time which is most pleasant and not merely that which is longest.
context: The quality of a life matters more than its length, just as we choose food for its taste, not its quantity.
prompt: How could you make today sweeter rather than longer?

text: Duty is the necessity of acting from respect for the law.
context: For Kant, duty isn't blind obedience. It means acting from respect for a principle you recognise as right.
prompt: Which principle do you keep even when nobody is watching?

text: Is it only when the flowers are in full bloom and when the moon is shining in spotless perfection that we ought to gaze at them? … The twigs which bear no blossoms as yet and a garden strewn with withered petals are equally to be admired.
context: Kenkō's most famous essay. Beauty isn't only in the peak moment, but in anticipation, in absence, and in what has already passed.
prompt: What 'not yet' or 'no longer' could you admire today?

text: The difficulty, my friends, is not to avoid death, but to avoid unrighteousness; for that runs faster than death.
context: Sentenced to die, Socrates observes that wrongdoing is the swifter pursuer. His accusers, he says, have been overtaken by it.
prompt: What wrong is easier to fall into than you'd like to admit?

text: Those only are happy (I thought) who have their minds fixed on some object other than their own happiness; on the happiness of others, on the improvement of mankind, even on some art or pursuit, followed not as a means, but as itself an ideal end. Aiming thus at something else, they find happiness by the way.
context: Mill's own recipe after his crisis: devote yourself to others, to improving the world, or to an art for its own sake, and happiness arrives on the way.
prompt: What could you fix your mind on that is bigger than your own happiness?

text: He who fights with monsters should be careful lest he thereby become a monster. And if thou gaze long into an abyss, the abyss will also gaze into thee.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil 146
context: A warning to anyone fighting something they despise: the struggle can reshape us into what we oppose.
prompt: Is something you are fighting changing you?

text: He acts before he speaks, and afterwards speaks according to his actions.
context: Asked what makes a person of true quality, Confucius points to the order of things: first do it, then talk about it.
prompt: What are you talking about doing that you could simply start?

text: Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good.
context: The Stoics used the awareness of death not to frighten but to focus: the time to be good is now, while it is still possible.
prompt: What good thing have you been postponing as if you had endless time?

text: It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to carry it when it is full. If you keep feeling a point that has been sharpened, the point cannot long preserve its sharpness.
context: Overfilling and oversharpening both defeat their purpose. Knowing when to stop is a skill.
prompt: What are you filling to the brim that would be better left with room?

text: Whether we are accustomed this way or that straight from childhood, makes not a small but an important difference, or rather I would say it makes all the difference.
context: Habits formed early shape the person we become. The same is true of the habits we form now.
prompt: Which habit from your childhood still shapes you, for better or worse?

text: By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.
context: The 'flood' in Buddhist imagery is the rush of craving and confusion. Steady effort builds an island where the mind can stand.
prompt: What practice could be your island this week?

text: We must remember that the future is neither wholly ours nor wholly not ours, so that neither must we count upon it as quite certain to come nor despair of it as quite certain not to come.
context: A balanced stance toward the future: neither counting on it nor despairing of it.
prompt: What are you either counting on or despairing of too much?

text: Should I be content that my maxim (to extricate myself from difficulty by a false promise) should hold good as a universal law, for myself as well as for others?
context: Kant's test for a lie told to escape a difficulty: would you accept a world where everyone lied whenever it suited them?
prompt: What small untruth would fail this test?

text: The art of life lies in a constant readjustment to our surroundings.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. III
context: Okakura draws on Taoism: there is no fixed recipe for living well, only continual, graceful adjustment.
prompt: What change around you are you resisting instead of adjusting to?

text: All the grand sources, in short, of human suffering are in a great degree, many of them almost entirely, conquerable by human care and effort.
context: Mill's hope: poverty, disease and much misfortune are not fate. Most suffering can be reduced by human effort, slowly but surely.
prompt: What suffering near you could your care and effort reduce?

text: Of all that is written, I love only what a person hath written with his blood. Write with blood, and thou wilt find that blood is spirit.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra I, 'Reading and Writing'
context: Nietzsche valued writing, and living, that come from genuine experience rather than borrowed opinion.
prompt: What could you say, or do, today that comes from your own blood?

text: Is virtue a thing remote? I wish to be virtuous, and lo! virtue is at hand.
context: Goodness is not far away, waiting for the perfect moment. It begins the instant we genuinely want it.
prompt: What good thing are you postponing that you could begin right now?

text: When thou art offended with any man's shameless conduct, immediately ask thyself, Is it possible, then, that shameless men should not be in the world? It is not possible. Do not, then, require what is impossible.
context: Expecting a world without difficult people only guarantees frustration. Marcus asks himself to expect them, and so to meet them calmly.
prompt: What are you demanding of others that is simply impossible?

text: "A man," replied Confucius, "does not seek to see himself in running water, but in still water. For only what is itself still can instil stillness into others."
context: Zhuangzi puts these words in the mouth of Confucius. We can only see ourselves clearly in water that is still.
prompt: How could you become still enough to see yourself clearly?

text: And of this nature Happiness is mostly thought to be, for this we choose always for its own sake, and never with a view to anything further.
context: We want money, honour and even pleasure partly for what they bring. Happiness is the one thing we want simply for itself.
prompt: What do you chase as a means that you have started treating as an end?

text: Well-makers lead the water (wherever they like); fletchers bend the arrow; carpenters bend a log of wood; wise people fashion themselves.
context: Every craft shapes its material. The wise treat their own character as the material to be shaped.
prompt: What part of yourself are you shaping right now?

text: Continuous pain does not last long in the flesh; on the contrary, pain, if extreme, is present a very short time, and even that degree of pain which barely outweighs pleasure in the flesh does not last for many days together.
context: Epicurus himself suffered from painful illness. His teaching was that severe pain is brief and long pain is bearable.
prompt: What pain have you endured that turned out more bearable than you feared?

text: Morality is not properly the doctrine how we should make ourselves happy, but how we should become worthy of happiness.
context: Ethics, for Kant, is not a recipe for happiness. It is about becoming the kind of person who deserves it.
prompt: What would make you more worthy of the happiness you want?

text: He who afflicts his whole life by spending it in the pursuit of riches and fame, leaving himself no leisure for quiet, is but a fool.
context: Kenkō's verdict on a life spent chasing wealth and reputation with no time left for stillness.
prompt: Is there enough leisure for quiet in your life?

text: Let us, then, take the argument as our guide, which has revealed to us that the best way of life is to practise justice and every virtue in life and death.
context: The closing words of the Gorgias. After a long and heated argument, Socrates concludes simply: practise justice and every virtue.
prompt: What would it mean to follow the argument wherever it leads?

text: From this moment my burden grew lighter. The oppression of the thought that all feeling was dead within me was gone. I was no longer hopeless: I was not a stock or a stone. I had still, it seemed, some of the material out of which all worth of character, and all capacity for happiness, are made.
context: Mill describes the moment his depression began to lift: reading a moving story, he cried, and realised he could still feel.
prompt: When did you last feel something deeply, and what did it tell you?

text: There is more sagacity in thy body than in thy best wisdom.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra I, 'The Despisers of the Body'
context: Against those who despise the body, Zarathustra insists it holds an intelligence of its own.
prompt: What is your body trying to tell you?

text: Learn as if you could not reach your object, and were always fearing also lest you should lose it.
context: Confucius describes the eager student: always reaching ahead, and holding on to what was learned as if it might slip away.
prompt: What are you learning that deserves this kind of eagerness?

text: Men exist for the sake of one another. Teach them then, or bear with them.
context: The Stoics saw humans as social by nature. When others fall short, there are only two fitting responses: help them see, or be patient.
prompt: Is there someone you could teach, or someone you need to bear with?

text: All in the world know the beauty of the beautiful, and in doing this they have (the idea of) what ugliness is; they all know the skill of the skilful, and in doing this they have (the idea of) what the want of skill is.
context: Every idea of 'good' quietly creates its opposite. Labels divide the world as much as they describe it.
prompt: Which label you use creates the very thing you dislike?

text: Where is the use of such prosperity if there be taken away the doing of kindnesses of which friends are the most usual and most commendable objects?
context: Wealth and power are worth little without friends to do good to, and are harder to keep without them.
prompt: What could you share today with someone you care about?

text: Wise people, after they have listened to the laws, become serene, like a deep, smooth, and still lake.
context: Understanding, once truly absorbed, does not agitate. It settles the mind like a still lake.
prompt: What would help your mind become a little more still today?

text: It is impossible to live a pleasant life without living wisely and well and justly, and it is impossible to live wisely and well and justly without living pleasantly.
context: Pleasure, wisdom and justice are bound together. None can be had fully without the others.
prompt: Which of the three is weakest in your life right now?

text: Ask him, however- if his sovereign ordered him, on pain of the same immediate execution, to bear false witness against an honourable man, whom the prince might wish to destroy under a plausible pretext, would he consider it possible in that case to overcome his love of life, however great it may be.
context: Kant's thought experiment: ordered on pain of death to bear false witness against an innocent person, could you refuse? You may not know whether you would, but you know you could.
prompt: What would you refuse to do, whatever it cost?

text: It is barely ten feet square, and only seven feet high. As it was not meant for a fixed abode, the ground about it was trodden hard and left uncultivated. The walls are of mud, and it is thatched with rushes. The joints are fastened with rings and staples, for the greater convenience of removal elsewhere if any subject of dissatisfaction should arise. How little trouble it would take to rebuild it in another place!
context: Chōmei's last home was a hut small enough to take apart and move on two carts. Owning little, he could not lose much.
prompt: What could you live without, and how would that lighten you?

text: Behold! human beings living in a underground den, which has a mouth open towards the light and reaching all along the den; here they have been from their childhood, and have their legs and necks chained so that they cannot move, and can only see before them, being prevented by the chains from turning round their heads.
context: The opening of the Allegory of the Cave. Prisoners mistake shadows on a wall for reality; philosophy is the slow, painful turn toward the light.
prompt: What shadows might you be mistaking for the real thing?

text: The happiness which forms the utilitarian standard of what is right in conduct, is not the agent's own happiness, but that of all concerned. As between his own happiness and that of others, utilitarianism requires him to be as strictly impartial as a disinterested and benevolent spectator.
context: Utilitarianism counts everyone's happiness equally, your own included but no more than anyone else's.
prompt: How would you decide if your own happiness counted no more than another's?

text: In a particular flower I may train myself to see the whole world; or I may listen to the many hints and suggestions which Nature offers with respect to human life.
context: The young Kierkegaard decides he does not need to master science to learn from nature. One flower, looked at closely, can teach a great deal.
prompt: What small thing near you could you look at long enough to learn from?

text: There were four things from which the Master was entirely free. He had no foregone conclusions, no arbitrary predeterminations, no obstinacy, and no egoism.
context: His students' portrait of Confucius: no fixed conclusions, no rigid plans, no stubbornness and no ego.
prompt: Which of the four do you hold on to most tightly?

text: In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present,—I am rising to the work of a human being.
context: Even an emperor struggled to get out of bed. His answer was to remember what he was for.
prompt: What work, worthy of a human being, is waiting for you today?

text: All things alike go through their processes of activity, and (then) we see them return (to their original state). When things (in the vegetable world) have displayed their luxuriant growth, we see each of them return to its root. This returning to their root is what we call the state of stillness.
context: Everything grows, flourishes and returns to its root, like plants through the seasons. Stillness is the return, not the absence of life.
prompt: What root do you need to return to?

text: It is requisite that they have kindly feelings towards one another, and wish one another good from one of the aforementioned causes, and that these kindly feelings should be mutually known.
context: Goodwill isn't enough for friendship; it has to be mutual, and both people have to know it.
prompt: Who might not know how much goodwill you feel toward them?

text: Even though a speech be a thousand (of words), but made up of senseless words, one word of sense is better, which if a man hears, he becomes quiet.
context: Quantity of words is not the measure. One true word that brings peace outweighs a thousand empty ones.
prompt: What one word of sense do you need to hear, or to say?

text: No pleasure is in itself evil, but the things which produce certain pleasures entail annoyances many times greater than the pleasures themselves.
context: The problem is never pleasure itself, but what certain pleasures bring along with them.
prompt: Which pleasure brings trouble along with it?

text: This is virtue, and virtue, at least as a naturally acquired faculty, can never be perfect.
context: Virtue, for Kant, is steady progress rather than a finished state.
prompt: Where are you making steady progress, even if you're not perfect?

text: Nothing is more hallowing than the union of kindred spirits in art. At the moment of meeting, the art lover transcends himself. At once he is and is not. He catches a glimpse of Infinity, but words cannot voice his delight, for the eye has no tongue.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. V
context: Okakura describes the moment when a work of art and its viewer truly meet, beyond words.
prompt: When did a piece of art last leave you without words?

text: Bodily exercise, when compulsory, does no harm to the body; but knowledge which is acquired under compulsion obtains no hold on the mind. … do not use compulsion, but let early education be a sort of amusement; you will then be better able to find out the natural bent.
context: Plato's view of education: learning forced on us does not last. Learning through play reveals who we really are.
prompt: What would you love to learn if no one were making you?

text: A person whose desires and impulses are his own—are the expression of his own nature, as it has been developed and modified by his own culture—is said to have a character. One whose desires and impulses are not his own, has no character, no more than a steam-engine has a character.
context: Character, for Mill, means desires that are genuinely your own, developed by your own reflection.
prompt: Which of your desires are truly your own?

text: “What is hell?” I maintain that it is the suffering of being unable to love.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book VI, ch. 3
context: From the teachings of the elder Zosima, gathered after his death. Hell is not a place but a condition: the loss of the capacity to love.
prompt: Where has your capacity to love grown thin?

text: It passes on just like this, not ceasing day or night!
context: Confucius, standing by a river. Like Heraclitus in Greece, he sees life flowing on without pause.
prompt: What is flowing past you right now that you would like to notice?

text: When thou wishest to delight thyself, think of the virtues of those who live with thee; for instance, the activity of one, and the modesty of another, and the liberality of a third, and some other good quality of a fourth.
context: A simple exercise in gratitude: notice the particular virtues of the people around you.
prompt: Name one good quality in each of three people close to you.

text: The softest thing in the world dashes against and overcomes the hardest; that which has no (substantial) existence enters where there is no crevice.
context: What is soft finds its way where the hard cannot. Gentleness has its own power.
prompt: Where could you go further by being gentler?

text: They improve also, as it seems, by repeated acts, and by mutual correction, for they receive impress from one another in the points which give them pleasure; whence says the Poet, “Thou from the good, good things shalt surely learn.”
context: Good friends make each other better, through time together and honest correction. Aristotle closes his books on friendship with this thought.
prompt: Who makes you better, and how?

text: All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter.
context: The ethic of non-harm rests on a simple act of imagination: others fear pain and death just as we do.
prompt: Whose fear could you understand better by putting yourself in their place?

text: Fortune but seldom interferes with the wise man; his greatest and highest interests have been, are, and will be, directed by reason throughout the course of his life.
context: Luck affects the outer edges of a life. What matters most is guided by our own reasoning.
prompt: What part of your life is governed by reason rather than luck?

text: The notion of happiness is so indefinite that although every man wishes to attain it, yet he never can say definitely and consistently what it is that he really wishes and wills.
context: Everyone wants happiness, Kant observes, yet nobody can say exactly what it would consist of. It is too tied to changing experience to be a firm guide.
prompt: If you had to say precisely what would make you happy, could you?

text: How can a man ever find it wearisome to live at leisure? Free from surrounding cares, it is good merely to be alone.
context: Kenkō defends solitude: away from the noise of the world, we stop being blown about by everyone else's moods.
prompt: When did you last enjoy being alone?

text: Old age has a great sense of calm and freedom; when the passions relax their hold, then, as Sophocles says, we are freed from the grasp not of one mad master only, but of many.
context: The elderly Cephalus, at the opening of the Republic, finds that age has freed him from the tyranny of his passions.
prompt: What passion would you be glad to be free of?

text: In them I seemed to draw from a source of inward joy, of sympathetic and imaginative pleasure, which could be shared in by all human beings.
context: Wordsworth's poems helped heal Mill. In them he found a joy that excluded no one.
prompt: What gives you a joy that anyone could share?

text: Love in action is a harsh and dreadful thing compared with love in dreams.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book II, ch. 4
context: Zosima to a woman who dreams of serving humanity but cannot bear ingratitude. Real love is slow, unglamorous and costly.
prompt: Where is your love still in dreams, and where is it in action?

text: The prosecution of learning may be compared to what may happen in raising a mound. If there want but one basket of earth to complete the work, and I stop, the stopping is my own work. It may be compared to throwing down the earth on the level ground. Though but one basketful is thrown at a time, the advancing with it is my own going forward.
context: Building a mound one basket at a time: whether we stop just short or keep adding, the choice is always ours.
prompt: What are you one basket away from finishing, or from starting?

text: Since it is possible that thou mayest depart from life this very moment, regulate every act and thought accordingly.
context: Not a counsel of fear, but of seriousness: live as one who knows life is not guaranteed.
prompt: Which of today's acts would you do differently in that light?

text: It is wood of no quality, and of no use. That is why it has attained its present age.
context: A carpenter dismisses a huge old tree as worthless. That evening the tree appears in his dream: being 'useless' is what let it grow so old.
prompt: What 'useless' thing in your life is actually keeping you whole?

text: Time is a good discoverer and co-operator in such matters: it is thus in fact that all improvements in the various arts have been brought about, for any man may fill up a deficiency.
context: Aristotle sketches his ideas and leaves room for others to improve them. Understanding grows over time and through many hands.
prompt: What idea of yours could someone else help you improve?

text: Do not speak harshly to anybody; those who are spoken to will answer thee in the same way. Angry speech is painful, blows for blows will touch thee.
context: Harsh speech returns to the speaker. The verse is practical before it is moral.
prompt: What tone have you been using with the people around you?

text: The just man enjoys the greatest peace of mind, while the unjust is full of the utmost disquietude.
context: For Epicurus, justice is valuable partly because it lets us sleep at night.
prompt: Is there anything on your conscience disturbing your peace?

text: A man must first appreciate the importance of what we call duty, the authority of the moral law, and the immediate dignity which the following of it gives to the person in his own eyes.
context: The satisfaction of doing right only comes once we've recognised for ourselves why it matters.
prompt: Which duty brings you a quiet sense of dignity?

text: He only who has lived with the beautiful can die beautifully.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. VII
context: Okakura writes of the great tea masters, who met even their deaths with the grace they had practised all their lives.
prompt: What beauty are you living with every day?

text: He who is of a calm and happy nature will hardly feel the pressure of age, but to him who is of an opposite disposition youth and age are equally a burden.
context: Cephalus again: what makes a life heavy is not age but temperament.
prompt: What in your temperament makes life lighter, or heavier?

text: Few human creatures would consent to be changed into any of the lower animals, for a promise of the fullest allowance of a beast's pleasures.
context: Mill's argument for higher pleasures: almost nobody would trade a human life for an animal's, however comfortable.
prompt: What makes your life worth more to you than comfort?

text: Every one is really responsible to all men for all men and for everything.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book VI, ch. 2
context: Spoken by Zosima's dying brother Markel, who in his last days discovers a joyful sense of connection to everyone.
prompt: What would change if you felt responsible for those around you?

text: The commander of the forces of a large state may be carried off, but the will of even a common man cannot be taken from him.
context: An army can lose its general, but no one can take away a person's will. Even the most ordinary life holds this inner freedom.
prompt: What choice is entirely yours today, whatever happens around you?

text: How much trouble he avoids who does not look to see what his neighbor says or does or thinks, but only to what he does himself.
context: Much unrest comes from monitoring others. Marcus turns his attention back to his own conduct.
prompt: Whose life have you been watching instead of tending your own?

text: He who knows (the Tao) does not (care to) speak (about it); he who is (ever ready to) speak about it does not know it.
context: Often quoted as 'those who know do not speak; those who speak do not know'. Deep understanding tends to be quiet.
prompt: What do you understand best, and how little do you need to say about it?

text: Man is by nature adapted to a social existence.
context: A good life is never lived entirely alone. For Aristotle, our nature is social.
prompt: Which relationships are part of your good life?

text: Let each man direct himself first to what is proper, then let him teach others; thus a wise man will not suffer.
context: Before guiding others, first set oneself on the right course.
prompt: What advice you often give could you take yourself?

text: Unlimited time and limited time afford an equal amount of pleasure, if we measure the limits of that pleasure by reason.
context: A complete life is not measured by its length. Understood rightly, a finite life can be whole.
prompt: What would make your life feel complete, regardless of its length?

text: Put the case that the mind of that philanthropist were clouded by sorrow of his own, extinguishing all sympathy with the lot of others, and that, while he still has the power to benefit others in distress, he is not touched by their trouble because he is absorbed with his own; and now suppose that he tears himself out of this dead insensibility, and performs the action without any inclination to it, but simply from duty, then first has his action its genuine moral worth.
context: Kant imagines a kind person whose own grief has numbed their sympathy, yet who helps others anyway. That, he says, is where moral worth truly shows.
prompt: Who could you help today even if you don't feel like it?

text: He who mixes with the experts while he is himself still stiff and imperfect, and is not ashamed when others laugh and mock at him, will enjoy overcoming such discouragement; and, though he have not the natural talent for it, he will not lag far behind the others.
context: Waiting until we're good before practising in public means never getting good. Kenkō recommends being a beginner openly.
prompt: What are you avoiding because you're not good at it yet?

text: The power and capacity of learning exists in the soul already; and that just as the eye was unable to turn from darkness to light without the whole body, so too the instrument of knowledge can only by the movement of the whole soul be turned from the world of becoming into that of being.
context: Education, for Plato, is not pouring knowledge into an empty vessel but turning the whole soul toward the light.
prompt: What understanding is already in you, waiting to be turned toward?

text: The dictum that truth always triumphs over persecution, is one of those pleasant falsehoods which men repeat after one another till they pass into commonplaces, but which all experience refutes.
context: It's comforting to believe truth always wins. Mill warns that history says otherwise: it needs defending.
prompt: Which truth could use your defending?

text: The more I love humanity in general, the less I love man in particular.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book II, ch. 4
context: Zosima recalls a doctor's confession: loving humanity in the abstract is easy; loving the person in front of us is hard.
prompt: Who is the particular person you find hardest to love?

text: When the year becomes cold, then we know how the pine and the cypress are the last to lose their leaves.
context: Pines and cypresses stay green through winter. Character, like an evergreen, shows itself in the hard seasons.
prompt: Who stayed green for you during a hard winter?

text: Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.
context: Epictetus does not ask us to stop caring, but to stop demanding that reality match our wishes.
prompt: What would you accept today if you stopped arguing with it?

text: Great knowledge embraces the whole: small knowledge, a part only.
context: Small knowledge sees a part and takes it for everything. Great knowledge keeps the whole in view.
prompt: What part of a situation have you been mistaking for the whole?

text: The man who flies from and fears all things, and never stands up against anything, comes to be a coward; and he who fears nothing, but goes at everything, comes to be rash.
context: Courage is the mean between cowardice and recklessness, and both extremes are formed by habit.
prompt: Are you leaning toward fear or toward recklessness lately?

text: Self is the lord of self, who else could be the lord? With self well subdued, a man finds a lord such as few can find.
context: No one else can master our mind for us. Self-reliance is at the heart of the Buddha's teaching.
prompt: Where are you waiting for someone else to change what only you can?

text: He who understands the limits of life knows how easy it is to procure enough to remove the pain of want and make the whole of life complete and perfect. Hence he has no longer any need of things which are not to be won save by labour and conflict.
context: Knowing how little we truly need frees us from struggles that were never necessary.
prompt: Which of your struggles is for something you don't really need?

text: For love, as an affection, cannot be commanded, but beneficence for duty's sake may; even though we are not impelled to it by any inclination- nay, are even repelled by a natural and unconquerable aversion.
