context: Feelings can't be ordered, says Kant, but kindness can. 'Practical love' lives in what we choose to do, not in what we happen to feel.
prompt: Who could you treat with love today, even without feeling it?

text: "Young fool," chided the tea-master, "that is not the way a garden path should be swept." Saying this, Rikiu stepped into the garden, shook a tree and scattered over the garden gold and crimson leaves, scraps of the brocade of autumn!
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. IV
context: The tea master Rikyū's lesson to a son who had swept the garden perfectly clean: real beauty needs a touch of the natural.
prompt: Where could you allow a few leaves to fall?

text: He sets in order his own inner life, and is his own master and his own law, and at peace with himself.
context: Plato's definition of justice in the soul: each part doing its own work, in harmony, like notes in a scale.
prompt: What would it take to be at peace with yourself today?

text: Its most appropriate appellation is a sense of dignity, which all human beings possess in one form or other.
context: Why would anyone prefer a harder, nobler life? Mill's answer: a sense of dignity that every human being has in some form.
prompt: What would you never do because of your own sense of dignity?

text: What is a poet? A poet is an unhappy creature; his heart is torn by secret sufferings, but his lips are so formed that when the cries and the sighs escape them, they create a sound of beautiful music.
context: The opening aphorism of Either/Or (1843), in the voice of a young aesthete. Beautiful art can hide real pain, and admirers rarely ask what it costs.
prompt: Whose cheerful surface might be hiding something you haven't asked about?

text: To go beyond is as wrong as to fall short.
context: Asked which of two students was better, one who overdid things and one who fell short, Confucius refused to choose. The ideal is the balanced middle, the due mean, much like Aristotle's.
prompt: Where are you overdoing something, and where falling short?

text: Never say about anything, I have lost it, but say I have restored it.
context: Everything we hold is on loan. Speaking of 'returning' rather than 'losing' changes how we hold what we have while we have it.
prompt: What do you hold that you could hold more lightly, and more gratefully?

text: But I have three precious things which I prize and hold fast. The first is gentleness; the second is economy; and the third is shrinking from taking precedence of others.
context: Laozi's three treasures: gentleness, frugality, and not needing to be first.
prompt: Which of the three treasures could you practise today?

text: For the very presence of friends is pleasant even in adversity: since men when grieved are comforted by the sympathy of their friends.
context: Aristotle wonders whether friends really share our burdens, or whether their company simply makes the pain lighter. Either way, they help.
prompt: Whose presence could you offer to someone going through a hard time?

text: By oneself the evil is done, by oneself one suffers; by oneself evil is left undone, by oneself one is purified. Purity and impurity belong to oneself, no one can purify another.
context: Responsibility is personal: no one can do our wrong for us, and no one can make us pure in our place.
prompt: What is yours alone to take responsibility for?

text: All such desires as lead to no pain when they remain ungratified are unnecessary, and the longing is easily got rid of, when the thing desired is difficult to procure or when the desires seem likely to produce harm.
context: A test for any desire: would going without it actually hurt? If not, it can be let go.
prompt: Which desire would cost you nothing to give up?

text: Intelligence, wit, judgement, and the other talents of the mind, however they may be named, or courage, resolution, perseverance, as qualities of temperament, are undoubtedly good and desirable in many respects; but these gifts of nature may also become extremely bad and mischievous if the will which is to make use of them, and which, therefore, constitutes what is called character, is not good.
context: Talents and courage are gifts, but in a bad will they become dangerous. Character is what decides how they're used.
prompt: Which of your gifts depends on good will to stay good?

text: You may propose to do a certain thing to-day, but some unforeseen matter of importance crops up and you spend the time wrongly on it; or perhaps somebody you had expected cannot come, and some unexpected visitor arrives instead. At all events you fail to do what you had planned, and it is only the unlooked for that actually happens.
context: Kenkō on plans: the day rarely goes as expected, and neither do years. Better to hold plans lightly.
prompt: What unexpected thing happened today, and what did it bring?

text: He who is the real tyrant, whatever men may think, is the real slave.
context: The tyrant seems to have everything, but is ruled by desires he can never satisfy.
prompt: Which of your desires rules you more than you rule it?

text: However true it may be, if it is not fully, frequently, and fearlessly discussed, it will be held as a dead dogma, not a living truth.
context: Even true beliefs go stale when they're never questioned. Discussion keeps them alive.
prompt: Which of your beliefs have you not examined in a long time?

text: Let us be, first and above all, kind, then honest and then let us never forget each other!
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Epilogue, ch. 3
context: The closing scene of the novel. After all its darkness, Dostoevsky ends with a simple order of priorities.
prompt: Who should you make sure never to forget?

text: When internal examination discovers nothing wrong, what is there to be anxious about, what is there to fear?
context: Asked about the person of true quality, Confucius says they live without anxiety or fear, not because life is safe but because their conscience is clear.
prompt: What would clear your conscience enough to let a worry go?

text: Remember that in life you ought to behave as at a banquet. Suppose that something is carried round and is opposite to you. Stretch out your hand and take a portion with decency. Suppose that it passes by you. Do not detain it.
context: Life passes things around like dishes at a dinner. Take your share with grace; don't grab, and don't cling to what moves on.
prompt: What is passing by you that you are trying to hold onto?

text: Man at his birth is supple and weak; at his death, firm and strong. (So it is with) all things. Trees and plants, in their early growth, are soft and brittle; at their death, dry and withered. Thus it is that firmness and strength are the concomitants of death; softness and weakness, the concomitants of life.
context: Living things bend; dead things are rigid. Flexibility is a sign of life, in bodies and in minds.
prompt: Where have you grown rigid, and how could you soften?

text: Whatever is proper to each is naturally best and pleasantest to him: such then is to Man the life in accordance with pure Intellect (since this Principle is most truly Man), and if so, then it is also the happiest.
context: Each creature flourishes by doing what is most its own. For humans, Aristotle thought, that means a life of thought and understanding.
prompt: What activity makes you feel most yourself?

text: Let us live happily then, not hating those who hate us! among men who hate us let us dwell free from hatred!
context: From the chapter on happiness. Happiness here is not the absence of hostility, but freedom from returning it.
prompt: What would it feel like to live free from hatred, even toward one person?

text: Of our desires some are natural and necessary; others are natural, but not necessary; others, again, are neither natural nor necessary, but are due to illusory opinion.
context: Epicurus' famous threefold sorting of desires. An ancient commentator gives examples: drink when thirsty; fine food; crowns and statues in one's honour.
prompt: Sort three of your current desires into these three kinds.

text: To secure one's own happiness is a duty, at least indirectly; for discontent with one's condition, under a pressure of many anxieties and amidst unsatisfied wants, might easily become a great temptation to transgression of duty.
context: Kant isn't against happiness: neglecting our own wellbeing makes it harder to act well.
prompt: How is looking after yourself part of doing right?

text: One cannot listen to different pieces of music at the same time, a real comprehension of the beautiful being possible only through concentration upon some central motive.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. IV
context: The tea room displays one beautiful object at a time. Okakura's point applies to attention in general.
prompt: What one thing deserves your full attention today?

text: Human nature was originally one and we were a whole, and the desire and pursuit of the whole is called love.
context: From Aristophanes' speech: humans were once whole beings, split in two, and love is the longing to be whole again.
prompt: What makes you feel whole?

text: The maintenance of a due balance among the faculties now seemed to be of primary importance. The cultivation of the feelings became one of the cardinal points in my ethical and philosophical creed.
context: After his crisis, Mill decided that reason alone was not enough; feelings needed cultivating too, through poetry, art and nature.
prompt: Which side of you, thinking or feeling, needs more attention?

text: Man is fond of reckoning up his troubles, but does not count his joys. If he counted them up as he ought, he would see that every lot has enough happiness provided for it.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, Notes from Underground II, ch. 6
context: Spoken by the bitter narrator of Notes from Underground, yet true: we tally our troubles and forget our joys.
prompt: What joys could you count today?

text: To be poor without murmuring is difficult. To be rich without being proud is easy.
context: Confucius is honest about which test is harder. Grace in hardship asks far more of us than modesty in comfort.
prompt: What difficulty could you carry today without complaining about it?

text: Remember that it is not he who reviles you or strikes you, who insults you, but it is your opinion about these things as being insulting. When then a man irritates you, you must know that it is your own opinion which has irritated you.
context: Insults wound only when we agree with them inwardly. Epictetus hands the power back to the one being insulted.
prompt: Whose words have you allowed to irritate you, and could you take that permission back?

text: My life has a limit, but my knowledge is without limit. To drive the limited in search of the limitless, is fatal; and the knowledge of those who do this is fatally lost.
context: Zhuangzi's warning against trying to know everything. A finite life spent chasing the infinite runs out.
prompt: What are you trying to master that could never be finished?

text: It is thought then to be the property of the Practically Wise man to be able to deliberate well respecting what is good and expedient for himself, not in any definite line, as what is conducive to health or strength, but what to living well.
context: Practical wisdom (phronesis) is the skill of judging well about life as a whole, not just about one narrow goal.
prompt: What decision are you facing that calls for wisdom about life as a whole?

text: Victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is unhappy. He who has given up both victory and defeat, he, the contented, is happy.
context: Every victory creates a loser, and the loser's bitterness. Contentment lies beyond the game of winning and losing.
prompt: Where are you trying to win when you could simply let go?

text: On this blissful day, which is also the last of my life, I write this to you. My continual sufferings from strangury and dysentery are so great that nothing could augment them; but over against them all I set gladness of mind at the remembrance of our past conversations.
context: Written by Epicurus on the day he died, in great pain. Memories of friendship and conversation outweighed everything else.
prompt: Which conversations would you want to remember at the end?

text: If we look closer at them we everywhere come upon the dear self which is always prominent, and it is this they have in view and not the strict command of duty which would often require self-denial.
context: Kant admits that most of our good actions are mixed with self-interest. 'The dear self' is always somewhere nearby.
prompt: Where is the dear self hiding in your good deeds?

text: Many are the things on which we should place no reliance; for it is because he had had such complete confidence in them that a foolish man feels angry and resentful (when they fail him). Have you power and authority? trust not in them; even the most dread personage may be overthrown. Have you riches? trust not in them; in an instant of time they may all be lost.
context: Kenkō lists the things we lean on (power, wealth, cleverness) and reminds us how quickly each can fail.
prompt: What are you relying on that could change in an instant?

text: “This, my dear Socrates,” said the stranger of Mantineia, “is that life above all others which man should live, in the contemplation of beauty absolute.”
context: The priestess Diotima teaches Socrates that love climbs from beautiful bodies to beautiful souls, ideas, and finally beauty itself.
prompt: Where did you notice beauty today?

text: All silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility.
context: Shutting down a conversation assumes we cannot be wrong.
prompt: Which conversation have you shut down because you were sure?

text: What man wants is simply independent choice, whatever that independence may cost and wherever it may lead.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, Notes from Underground I, ch. 7
context: The Underground Man argues that people are not calculating machines: above all, we want to choose for ourselves. Sartre would later argue that freedom is not optional: we cannot avoid choosing, even by doing nothing.
prompt: Where are you choosing freely, and where just following?

text: In ancient times, men learned with a view to their own improvement. Now-a-days, men learn with a view to the approbation of others.
context: A complaint from 2,500 years ago that sounds very modern: learning to grow, versus learning to impress.
prompt: Is there something you study mainly so that others will notice?

text: When any person treats you ill or speaks ill of you, remember that he does this or says this because he thinks that it is his duty. It is not possible then for him to follow that which seems right to you, but that which seems right to himself. … you will be mild in temper to him who reviles you; for say on each occasion, It seemed so to him.
context: People act on what seems right to them. Remembering this softens anger without excusing the act.
prompt: Who has acted on how things seemed to them, and can you see it from there?

text: The farther that one goes out (from himself), the less he knows.
context: Laozi's paradox for a restless age: understanding is not always found by going further.
prompt: What could you understand by staying where you are?

text: The happy man lives well and does well, for it has been stated by us to be pretty much a kind of living well and doing well.
context: Happiness, for Aristotle, is active: something we do, not just something we feel.
prompt: What would living well and doing well mean for you this week?

text: Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness.
context: A list of what truly counts as wealth. Nirvana is the Buddhist name for the final peace beyond craving.
prompt: By this measure, how rich are you today?

text:
The nations wax, the nations wane away;
In a brief space the generations pass,
And like to runners hand the lamp of life
One unto other.
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things II
context: Lucretius pictures the generations as relay runners, each handing the torch of life to the next.
prompt: What are you carrying that you hope to hand on?

text: Everything in nature works according to laws. Rational beings alone have the faculty of acting according to the conception of laws, that is according to principles, i.e., have a will.
context: Stones fall and rivers flow by law. People alone can act according to principles they understand, and that is what it means to have a will.
prompt: Which principle do you choose to live by?

text: When I first took up my abode in this place, I thought it was only for a little while. But five years have passed and my temporary hut has become old. Under the eaves there is a deep bed of withered leaves, and moss has gathered on the earthen floor.
context: Chōmei meant his hut to be temporary. Five years later, moss covers the floor. Life settles in while we're still telling ourselves it's for a little while.
prompt: What 'temporary' arrangement in your life has quietly become permanent?

text: For wisdom is a most beautiful thing, and Love is of the beautiful; and therefore Love is also a philosopher or lover of wisdom, and being a lover of wisdom is in a mean between the wise and the ignorant.
context: Love, in Diotima's account, is neither wise nor ignorant but always reaching: the very definition of a philosopher.
prompt: What are you reaching for that you don't yet have?

text: The internal sanction of duty, whatever our standard of duty may be, is one and the same—a feeling in our own mind; a pain, more or less intense, attendant on violation of duty.
context: Beyond laws and reputation, our strongest guard is conscience: the inner discomfort we feel when we fall short.
prompt: What is your conscience telling you at the moment?

text: Man is but a reed, the most feeble thing in nature; but he is a thinking reed.
context: Perhaps Pascal's most famous line. Human beings are fragile, but our capacity to think gives us a dignity the universe lacks. Camus would later call the clash between our need for meaning and a silent universe 'the absurd'.
prompt: How are you using your thinking today?

text: With what then will you recompense kindness? Recompense injury with justice, and recompense kindness with kindness.
context: Someone asks whether we should repay injury with kindness. Confucius replies with a question: then what is left for those who are kind to us? Fairness for harm, kindness for kindness.
prompt: Where would fairness serve better than forced kindness, or the other way round?

text: Everything has two handles, the one by which it may be borne, the other by which it may not. If your brother acts unjustly, do not lay hold of the act by that handle wherein he acts unjustly, for this is the handle which cannot be borne; but lay hold of the other, that he is your brother.
context: Every situation can be picked up in a way that can be carried or a way that cannot. We choose the handle.
prompt: Which handle are you holding a difficult relationship by?

text: When she died, I could not help being affected by her death. … passing from one phase to another like the sequence of spring, summer, autumn, and winter.
context: When Zhuangzi's wife dies, his friend finds him singing and drumming on a bowl. He grieved, he explains, and then saw her death as part of nature's turning seasons.
prompt: Which ending in your life could you see as a change of season?

text: Neither in prosperity will he be overjoyed nor in adversity will he be unduly pained.
context: From the portrait of the 'great-souled' person, who is steady because they know what really matters.
prompt: What would it take to be steadier through ups and downs?

text: He who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot, him I call a real driver; other people are but holding the reins.
context: Anger is pictured as a runaway chariot. The real driver is the one who can stop it.
prompt: When did you last hold back anger, and how did it feel afterwards?

text:
And in fee-simple life is given to none,
But unto all mere usufruct. Look back:
Nothing to us was all fore-passed eld
Of time the eternal, ere we had a birth.
And Nature holds this like a mirror up
Of time-to-be when we are dead and gone.
And what is there so horrible appears?
Now what is there so sad about it all?
Is't not serener far than any sleep?
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III
context: Life is lent, not owned. And the eternity after death, Lucretius argues, is no more frightening than the eternity before birth.
prompt: If life is on loan, how do you want to use it?

text: Tell him the history of an honest man whom men want to persuade to join the calumniators of an innocent and powerless person (say Anne Boleyn, accused by Henry VIII of England). He is offered advantages, great gifts, or high rank; he rejects them.
context: Kant suggests teaching ethics to children through stories like this one, where an honest man refuses bribes to join in slandering an innocent person.
prompt: Which story of honesty has stayed with you?

text: Generally speaking, uniformity in anything at all is bad; it is better to leave a little imperfection.
context: Kenkō praises frayed silk covers and mismatched books. Perfection, he suggests, leaves nothing to grow into.
prompt: Where could a little imperfection make something better?

text: Give me beauty in the inward soul; and may the outward and inward man be at one. May I reckon the wise to be the wealthy, and may I have such a quantity of gold as a temperate man and he only can bear and carry.
context: Socrates' prayer at the end of the Phaedrus: inner beauty, harmony between inner and outer life, and only as much wealth as a temperate person can carry.
prompt: How could your outward life better match your inward one?

text: The habit of analysis has a tendency to wear away the feelings: as indeed it has, when no other mental habit is cultivated, and the analysing spirit remains without its natural complements and correctives.
context: Mill, trained from childhood as a reasoning machine, discovered that constant analysis can dry up feeling unless balanced by other habits.
prompt: What are you over-analysing that might simply need feeling?

text: We smile at the life of the cloister, and yet no hermit ever lived so unreal a life as is common today, for the hermit did indeed abstract from the whole world, but he did not abstract from himself.
context: Kierkegaard mocks thinkers who build grand systems and forget that they are living people too. The hermit leaves the world; the pure thinker leaves himself.
prompt: Where do you think about life in a way that leaves you out of it?

text: He who requires much from himself and little from others, will keep himself from being the object of resentment.
context: High standards for ourselves, generous ones for others: a simple recipe for fewer grudges, in both directions.
prompt: Whom are you holding to a higher standard than you hold yourself?

text: If you would be a good reader, read; if a writer, write.
context: From a discourse on how habits are formed: every capacity is strengthened by its corresponding action, and weakened by neglect.
prompt: What do you want to become, and did you practise it today?

text: The more that he expends for others, the more does he possess of his own.
context: Generosity, says Laozi, does not empty us. What we give away somehow enlarges what we have.
prompt: What could you give today that would leave you richer?

text: To be a good man one must do each act in a particular frame of mind, I mean from Moral Choice and for the sake of the things themselves which are done.
context: Doing the right thing for the wrong reason isn't quite virtue. Goodness includes choosing the good for its own sake.
prompt: What good thing are you doing, and why are you really doing it?

text: Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!
context: Each quality is overcome by its opposite: anger by love, evil by good, greed by generosity, lies by truth.
prompt: Which opposite does a situation in your life call for?

text:
The man who sickens of his home goes out,
Forth from his splendid halls, and straight—returns,
Feeling i'faith no better off abroad.
He races, driving his Gallic ponies along,
Down to his villa, madly,—as in haste
To hurry help to a house afire.—At once
He yawns, as soon as foot has touched the threshold,
Or drowsily goes off in sleep and seeks
Forgetfulness, or maybe bustles about
And makes for town again. In such a way
Each human flees himself—a self in sooth,
As happens, he by no means can escape;
And willy-nilly he cleaves to it and loathes,
Sick, sick, and guessing not the cause of ail.
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III
context: A strikingly modern portrait of restlessness: the rich man rushing to his country house, bored on arrival, rushing back to town, always fleeing himself.
prompt: What are you running from by keeping busy?

text: Has not every even moderately honourable man sometimes found that, where by an otherwise inoffensive lie he might either have withdrawn himself from an unpleasant business, or even have procured some advantages for a loved and well-deserving friend, he has avoided it solely lest he should despise himself secretly in his own eyes?
context: Sometimes the only thing stopping a convenient lie is that we couldn't respect ourselves afterwards.
prompt: When did self-respect stop you from taking an easy way out?

text: It is hygiene, for it enforces cleanliness; it is economics, for it shows comfort in simplicity rather than in the complex and costly; it is moral geometry, inasmuch as it defines our sense of proportion to the universe.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. I
context: Okakura describes the tea ceremony as a whole way of life: cleanliness, simplicity, and a sense of our place in things.
prompt: Where could you choose the simple over the complex and costly?

text: Let the figure be composite—a pair of winged horses and a charioteer. … the human charioteer drives his in a pair; and one of them is noble and of noble breed, and the other is ignoble and of ignoble breed; and the driving of them of necessity gives a great deal of trouble to him.
context: Plato's image of the soul as a charioteer with two horses, one noble and one unruly. Reason must steer both.
prompt: Which of your horses has been pulling harder lately?

text: The utilitarian morality does recognise in human beings the power of sacrificing their own greatest good for the good of others. It only refuses to admit that the sacrifice is itself a good.
context: Mill honours self-sacrifice, but only when it actually helps someone. Suffering for its own sake, he says, is wasted.
prompt: Is a sacrifice you're making actually helping anyone?

text: So we never live, but we hope to live; and, as we are always preparing to be happy, it is inevitable we should never be so.
context: We live in memories and plans, rarely in the present. Always preparing to be happy, we never are.
prompt: What are you postponing being happy about?

text: What the superior man seeks, is in himself. What the mean man seeks, is in others.
context: The person of quality looks inward for causes and remedies; the petty person looks for someone else to blame.
prompt: What are you seeking from others that you could find in yourself?

text: What is the first business of him who philosophizes? To throw away self-conceit. For it is impossible for a man to begin to learn that which he thinks that he knows.
context: Learning begins with humility. Whatever we think we already understand, we stop examining.
prompt: What do you think you already know that might be worth relearning?

text: For the perfect man employs his mind as a mirror. It grasps nothing: it refuses nothing. It receives, but does not keep.
context: A mirror reflects whatever comes and holds onto nothing. Zhuangzi offers it as a picture of a free mind.
prompt: What are you still holding that you could simply let pass through?

text: Men should have been trained straight from their childhood to receive pleasure and pain from proper objects, for this is the right education…
context: Aristotle quotes his teacher Plato: a good education teaches us to enjoy the right things, not just to know them.
prompt: Which good things have you learned to enjoy?

text: Let a wise man blow off the impurities of his self, as a smith blows off the impurities of silver one by one, little by little, and from time to time.
context: Purifying silver takes patient, repeated work. So does refining one's character.
prompt: What small impurity could you work on, little by little?

text:
Why not,
Even like a banqueter, depart the halls,
Laden with life? why not with mind content
Take now, thou fool, thy unafflicted rest?
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III
context: Nature speaks to someone afraid of dying: if your life has been good, why not leave it like a guest who has dined well?
prompt: What would it mean to feel 'laden with life'?

text: When an upright man is in the greatest distress, which he might have avoided if he could only have disregarded duty, is he not sustained by the consciousness that he has maintained humanity in its proper dignity in his own person and honoured it, that he has no reason to be ashamed of himself in his own sight, or to dread the inward glance of self-examination?
context: Doing right may cost us dearly. What remains is the dignity of being able to look at ourselves honestly.
prompt: What would let you face your own honest gaze tonight?

text: The moon when full begins to wane; where there has been increase there is bound to be decrease; and in every case he who has reached the very front soon gets a set-back.
context: Kenkō on the danger of reaching the top: every peak is also the beginning of a descent.
prompt: Where could you be content with less than the very top?

text: This discovery of yours will create forgetfulness in the learners' souls, because they will not use their memories; they will trust to the external written characters and not remember of themselves. The specific which you have discovered is an aid not to memory, but to reminiscence, and you give your disciples not truth, but only the semblance of truth; they will be hearers of many things and will have learned nothing.
context: An Egyptian king warns the inventor of writing that it will weaken memory and give only the appearance of wisdom. The worry sounds familiar today.
prompt: What do you know only because it is stored somewhere, not in you?

text: Eccentricity has always abounded when and where strength of character has abounded; and the amount of eccentricity in a society has generally been proportional to the amount of genius, mental vigour, and moral courage which it contained.
context: Mill sees a society's tolerance of odd people as a sign of its vitality.
prompt: Where could you allow yourself to be a little more eccentric?

text: The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.
context: Pascal, a brilliant mathematician, insisted that not all knowing is logical. Some truths are felt before they are proven.
prompt: What does your heart know that your reason can't explain?

text: What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
context: Asked for one word to live by, Confucius chose shu, reciprocity, and summed it up in this line: a version of the golden rule found in many cultures.
prompt: Where today could you treat someone the way you would want to be treated?

text: Life is long enough, if you know how to use it.
source: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 2
context: Seneca's whole argument in one line: the problem is not the length of life but how we spend it.
prompt: What would 'using it well' look like this week?

text: Life is a loan with which the borrower does but add more dust and dirt to the sum total of existence. Life and death are as day and night.
context: Two disfigured men look at old tombs and talk calmly about mortality. Life, says one, is borrowed, and life and death follow each other like day and night.
prompt: If your life is a loan, what are you doing with it?

text: For Moral Virtue has for its object-matter pleasures and pains, because by reason of pleasure we do what is bad, and by reason of pain decline doing what is right.
context: Most of our failures come from chasing pleasure or avoiding discomfort. That's why virtue is mainly about training our likes and dislikes.
prompt: Which discomfort are you avoiding at the cost of doing right?

text: A man is not learned because he talks much; he who is patient, free from hatred and fear, he is called learned.
context: Real learning shows in character (patience, freedom from fear and hatred), not in how much one talks.
prompt: Where could you speak less and understand more?

text:
O wretched minds of men! O blinded hearts!
In how great perils, in what darks of life
Are spent the human years, however brief!—
O not to see that nature for herself
Barks after nothing, save that pain keep off,
Disjoined from the body, and that mind enjoy
Delightsome feeling, far from care and fear!
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things II
context: Lucretius laments how people waste their short lives striving for power, when nature asks only for freedom from pain and a mind at ease.
prompt: What does your nature actually ask of you today?

text: This word is self-contentment which in its proper signification always designates only a negative satisfaction in one's existence, in which one is conscious of needing nothing.
context: Kant's word for the quiet satisfaction of a good conscience: not pleasure, but the sense of needing nothing more.
prompt: When did you last feel that you needed nothing more?

text: When on a calm night the moon shines in at my window, I think with yearning of the men of old.
context: Alone in his hut, Chōmei finds company in the moon and in the memory of those who lived before him.
prompt: Who from the past do you feel close to on a quiet night?

text: How singular is the thing called pleasure, and how curiously related to pain, which might be thought to be the opposite of it; for they are never present to a man at the same instant, and yet he who pursues either is generally compelled to take the other; their bodies are two, but they are joined by a single head.
context: Socrates, his chains just removed on the day of his death, rubs his leg and reflects on how pleasure and pain always follow each other.
prompt: Which pleasure in your life always seems to bring its pain?

text: The demand that all other people shall resemble ourselves, grows by what it feeds on.
context: The urge to make others like us never stops on its own; every concession feeds it.
prompt: Where are you asking someone to be more like you?

text: The only thing which consoles us for our miseries is diversion, and yet this is the greatest of our miseries. For it is this which principally hinders us from reflecting upon ourselves, and which makes us insensibly ruin ourselves.
context: Pascal saw distraction as both comfort and trap: it keeps us from reflecting on our lives. (A typo in the source edition, 'it' for 'is', is corrected here.)
prompt: What distraction keeps you from reflecting on your life?

text: By nature, men are nearly alike; by practice, they get to be wide apart.
context: We start out much the same; what we do again and again makes us different. Aristotle would have agreed.
prompt: Which daily habit is quietly shaping who you are becoming?

text: You fear everything, like mortals as you are, and yet you desire everything as if you were immortals.
source: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 3
context: Seneca names a strange contradiction: we are anxious because we are mortal, yet we behave as if we had all the time in the world.
prompt: Which of your desires assumes you will live forever?

text: People in their conduct of affairs are constantly ruining them when they are on the eve of success.
context: Many projects fail at the very end, through carelessness when success is near. Laozi asks for the same care at the end as at the beginning.
prompt: What nearly finished thing deserves your full care now?

text: And Pleasure perfects the Working.
context: For Aristotle, pleasure is not opposed to good activity; it is what completes it and makes it whole.
prompt: Which of your good activities also bring you pleasure?

text: Through zeal knowledge is gotten, through lack of zeal knowledge is lost; let a man who knows this double path of gain and loss thus place himself that knowledge may grow.
context: Knowledge grows with effort and fades without it. The wise place themselves where it can grow.
prompt: Where could you put yourself so that your understanding grows?

text:
Since from amid the well-spring of delights
Bubbles some drop of bitter to torment
Among the very flowers…
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things IV
context: Even in the middle of pleasure, something bitter rises, often regret or unease of the mind.
prompt: What bitterness rises in you even amid good things?

text: Even the moral law itself in its solemn majesty is exposed to this endeavour to save oneself from yielding it respect.
context: We often look for a flaw in good people, and even in the moral law, so we don't have to feel humbled by them.
prompt: Whose goodness do you try to explain away?

text: The tea-room is unimpressive in appearance. It is smaller than the smallest of Japanese houses, while the materials used in its construction are intended to give the suggestion of refined poverty.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. IV
context: The tea room is deliberately tiny and plain, built to suggest 'refined poverty', and every humble detail is carefully chosen.
prompt: Where could plainness be a kind of refinement in your life?

text: Lest we become misologists, he replied, no worse thing can happen to a man than this. For as there are misanthropists or haters of men, there are also misologists or haters of ideas, and both spring from the same cause, which is ignorance of the world.
context: After an argument collapses, Socrates warns against giving up on reasoning altogether, just as disappointment can turn people against humanity.
prompt: Where has disappointment made you cynical?

text: Even in what people do for pleasure, conformity is the first thing thought of; they live in crowds; they exercise choice only among things commonly done: peculiarity of taste, eccentricity of conduct, are shunned equally with crimes: until by dint of not following their own nature, they have no nature to follow.
context: Mill's warning: by never following our own nature, we can end up with none to follow.
prompt: What would you enjoy if nobody else's taste mattered?

text: “I did that,” says my memory. “I could not have done that,” says my pride, and remains inexorable. Eventually—the memory yields.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil 68
context: A two-line portrait of self-deception: when memory and pride disagree, pride usually wins.
prompt: What has your pride persuaded your memory to forget?

text: The faults of the superior man are like the eclipses of the sun and moon. He has his faults, and all men see them; he changes again, and all men look up to him.
context: Zigong, a student of Confucius, on how a good person handles mistakes: openly, in full view, and then changed.
prompt: Which mistake of yours could you own more openly?

text: How late it is to begin life just when we have to be leaving it!
source: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 3
context: Said of people who plan to start living once they retire. Seneca's point: there is no later version of life waiting for you.

text: The mushroom of a morning knows not the alternation of day and night. The chrysalis knows not the alternation of spring and autumn.

text: The greatest remedy for anger is delay: beg anger to grant you this at the first, not in order that it may pardon the offence, but that it may form a right judgment about it: if it delays, it will come to an end.

text: The skilful traveller leaves no traces of his wheels or footsteps; the skilful speaker says nothing that can be found fault with or blamed.

text: Fear such things indeed he will, but he will stand up against them as he ought and as right reason may direct, with a view to what is honourable, because this is the end of the virtue.
